Sampling Shapley values of single predictions

Source: R/xpl.R
xpshap.Rd

Shares out one person's prediction among the inputs: the Shapley value of input j is its contribution averaged over every order in which the inputs could be revealed, the inputs not yet revealed taking values from the rows of x (the reference data). Strumbelj and Kononenko (2014) estimate it by sampling: each sample draws an order of the inputs and a row w of x, and takes the prediction at the person's values on j and the inputs before it (w's on the rest) less the prediction with j too taken from w. The value is the mean over nsamp samples, its standard error their standard deviation over sqrt(nsamp). Over all the inputs the values add up, in expectation, to the person's prediction less the mean prediction over x.

Usage

xpshap(
  x,
  f,
  newx = x[1L, , drop = FALSE],
  y = NULL,
  nsamp = 200,
  seed = 1,
  lctl = list()
)

# S3 method for class 'xpshap'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

The reference data: a numeric matrix, its column names those f sees, no missing values (the rows the learners in f are fitted to).

f

The prediction function: a function of a numeric matrix returning one finite number per row, or the names of learners of suplrn() ("glm", "lasso", "ridge", "enet", "forest").

newx

The rows to explain: a numeric matrix with the columns of x (by default its first row).

y

The outcome at the rows of x, needed only to fit the learners named in f.

nsamp

The samples of each value: one whole number from 1.

seed

The seed of the draws: one number, at least 0.

lctl

The settings of the learners named in f: a list named by arguments of suplrn() (fam, nfold, fold, disc, alpha, nlam, nfin, ntree, mtry, seed); empty for a function.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class xpshap, a list: phi and se, the values and their standard errors (one row per row of newx, one column per input); pred, the prediction at each row of newx; base, the mean prediction over the rows of x; and nsamp.

Details

The orders and rows are drawn in the compiled core from seed, the same on every platform; f is called once on all the rows.

References

Strumbelj, E. and Kononenko, I. (2014). Explaining prediction models and individual predictions with feature contributions. Knowledge and Information Systems, 41(3), 647-665. doi:10.1007/s10115-013-0679-x

Shapley, L. S. (1953). A value for n-person games. In Kuhn, H. W. and Tucker, A. W. (eds), Contributions to the Theory of Games II, 307-317. Princeton University Press.

Examples

set.seed(5)
x <- cbind(prior = rpois(100, 2), age = runif(100, 18, 60))
f <- function(m) plogis(-1 + 0.5 * m[, "prior"] - 0.03 * m[, "age"])
xpshap(x, f, newx = x[1:2, ], nsamp = 100)
#> xpshap: sampling Shapley values, 100 samples each; mean prediction 0.2695
#>        pred       prior         age
#>  0.09888651 -0.10661348 -0.06044138
#>  0.27926231  0.07142368 -0.05804795
